items.understanding: The book's value is that it forces readers to see academic theory applied to real-world commercial advertising.
items.cause: Pitting academic theories against actual commercial campaigns and field trials
items.effect: Readers are forced to see theory in the wild, making it a masterclass in structural analysis
items.asserted: The book bridges the ivory tower and the billboard by forcing us to see theory in the wild.

notAsserted.text: The theories are proven correct by the campaigns
notAsserted.why: The narration says we see theory in the wild, not that the theory is validated

notAsserted.text: The book is easy to read
notAsserted.why: No claim about difficulty or accessibility is made

keyFacts: The book bridges academic theory and commercial advertising
It is described as a masterclass in structural analysis
It forces us to see theory applied in real contexts
wrong: The billboard industry inspired the academic theories
Structural analysis is taught separately from advertising examples
The book is primarily a critique of ivory-tower thinking

items.understanding: A sign that simply stated a rule against stealing wood failed because it included no social proof about how common the theft was.
items.cause: The sign used an injunctive norm (stating the rule) but made no mention of theft frequency
items.effect: It provided no social proof, leaving a key persuasion mechanism unused
items.asserted: The injunctive-norm sign stated the rule but crucially omitted any reference to how often theft occurred, thus providing no social proof.

notAsserted.why: No outcome of this sign's effectiveness is stated in this narration

notAsserted.text: Social proof was present but ignored
notAsserted.why: The narration says social proof was absent, not ignored

keyFacts: The sign used an injunctive norm
It told people not to steal the wood
It made no mention of how often theft occurred
It provided no social proof
wrong: The sign included statistics about theft frequency
The sign's lack of social proof reduced theft rates
Cialdini's team wrote the sign to test social proof's presence

items.understanding: The speaker is about to object that something frustrates them regarding the von Restorff effect being a biological response.
items.cause: The von Restorff effect is a biological response (the established claim being referenced)
items.effect: The speaker interrupts to express frustration with that point
items.asserted: The speaker stops the conversation because the biological-response framing of the von Restorff effect frustrates them.

notAsserted.text: The von Restorff effect is NOT biological
notAsserted.why: The narration expresses frustration, not a counter-claim; the effect's nature is not settled here

notAsserted.text: The brand succeeded by being blue
notAsserted.why: Color is referenced contextually from prior narration, not asserted as the cause here

keyFacts: The von Restorff effect is described as a biological response
The speaker expresses frustration with this framing
The speaker interrupts to raise an objection
wrong: The speaker agrees that the von Restorff effect is purely biological
The brand failed because it chose to be the blue option
The speaker's frustration is about the brand's market success

items.understanding: Choosing the conventional, safe option (like IBM) protects a manager's career even if it fails, because failure by conformity is easier to justify than failure by innovation.
items.cause: IBM is the default safe choice; failing conventionally is safer for a middle manager's career
items.effect: It is infinitely safer to fail conventionally than unconventionally
items.asserted: Nobody ever got fired for buying IBM because conforming to the default is the safest career move for a middle manager.

notAsserted.why: The narration makes a career-safety argument, not a product-quality claim
The narration contrasts safety levels, not universal outcomes

keyFacts: IBM is cited as the default safe corporate choice
Failing conventionally is safer for a middle manager's career
The saying 'Nobody ever got fired for buying IBM' is a famous corporate adage
wrong: IBM became dominant because its products were superior
Middle managers who buy IBM are more likely to be promoted
Unconventional choices are safer for a manager's career than conventional ones

items.understanding: Despite the clumsy candidate's embarrassing coffee spill, the interviewer decides to hire them, which feels counterintuitive.
items.cause: The candidate spilled coffee and was clearly mortified
items.effect: The interviewer sits down and hires the clumsy candidate anyway, against intuition
items.asserted: You hire the clumsy candidate who spilled coffee, and the narration acknowledges this feels counterintuitive.

notAsserted.text: The clumsy candidate is objectively the best hire
notAsserted.why: The narration calls it counterintuitive, not objectively superior
The candidate is described as mortified, implying accident

keyFacts: The candidate spilled coffee on the carpet
The candidate was clearly mortified
The interviewer chose to hire the clumsy candidate
The decision is described as counterintuitive
wrong: The interviewer rejected the clumsy candidate because of the spill
The coffee spill improved the interviewer's confidence in the candidate rationally
The other candidate was hired instead

items.understanding: Casinos convert cash into chips to psychologically distance gamblers from real money, reducing the pain of loss and encouraging more spending.
items.cause: Casinos force players to convert cash into brightly colored plastic chips
items.effect: The loss is abstracted, the brain stops registering spending as giving up a real resource, friction disappears, and spending increases
items.asserted: Casinos use chips to abstract the loss so the brain treats money like Monopoly money, removing friction and enabling freer spending.

notAsserted.why: No fairness claim is made; the motivation given is psychological abstraction of loss

notAsserted.text: Players are unaware of chip conversion
notAsserted.why: The narration says casinos force conversion, implying players experience it

keyFacts: Casinos require cash to be converted into brightly colored plastic chips
Chips abstract the loss away from real money
The brain stops treating chips as a finite survival resource
Removing friction increases spending
wrong: Casinos use chips primarily for security and fraud prevention
Players spend less when using chips than cash
The chip system increases the brain's awareness of real financial loss
